definitions.definition: The operational structure and user's view of a system, evolved over time to include functional specification and hardware implementation; it defines the system-level building blocks.
A complete system integrated on a single die from interconnected components: processors (core, multimedia, coprocessors), memories, and interconnects.
A processor with an instruction set customized for a specific application or domain, sitting between custom ASIC hardware and software on general-purpose processors.
A device containing an array of computation units, memories, and interconnections, all programmable in the field by the user.
Coarse-Grained Reconfigurable Architecture, containing logic blocks that process byte-wide or multiple byte-wide data, forming the building blocks of datapaths.
ILP is a measure of how many operations in a computer program can be performed simultaneously, provided there is no data dependency among them.
An approach to exploit parallelism by concurrently performing different phases (fetch, decode, execute, etc.) of instruction processing, assuming these phases are independent.
A processor that dynamically examines the instruction stream to find independent operations, using multiple functional units and a scheduling window to process several instructions per cycle.
A processor relying on static compiler analysis to schedule independent operations into wide (≥64-bit) instruction words, with one operation field per execution unit.
A set of parallel processing elements connected via one or more networks, each with its own private local memory, operating on data distributed in a regular fashion.
A single processing unit resembling a traditional single-stream machine except that some functional units and registers operate on arrays of data values and are deeply pipelined.
A memory facility (often supported by an MMU) that enables programs requiring larger storage than the physical memory, so memory can be efficiently and securely accessed.
A predesigned circuit module that SOC technology interconnects to form a complete system, raising the design task from circuit level to system level.
An interconnect consisting of an array of switches (dynamically switched crossbar or statically switched 2-D mesh) that exchanges data packets, giving higher throughput than a bus-based system.
Average cost per chip, equal to total project cost divided by number of chips, where project cost is fixed cost Kf plus variable cost Kv × n.
An IP core implemented using the logic primitives of an FPGA; a microprocessor core entirely implemented by logic synthesis with a high degree of flexibility and configurability.
The unit of area measurement (rbe), defined as a six-transistor register cell including larger transistors, their interconnections, and inter-bit isolating spaces.
A set of control status information specified by a typical instruction set, including condition codes (positive, negative, zero, overflow) set by an instruction.
An instruction set, as in RISC, requiring arguments in registers before execution, with ALU instructions using register operands; regular and easy to decode.
An instruction set where instructions operate on operands in registers or with one operand in memory; uses fewer, variable-size instructions but makes decoding more difficult.
A unit that ensures the concurrent execution of multiple instructions has the same result as if the instructions were executed completely serially.
In-order instruction execution time as a linear sum: TTOTAL = TEXEC + TD + TM (execution, pipeline delays, memory delays).
A table storing a branch's target instruction and address, so a correctly guessed branch has zero delay; typically 70–98% effective, e.g. with 512 entries.
Dynamic branch prediction using a 2-bit saturating counter of taken/not-taken history: predict not-taken for 00, 01 and taken for 10, 11.
Hardware storage (VR) that decouples arithmetic processing from memory, serving as source and destination for all array operands, often bypassing the cache.
Elimination of WAR and WAW hazards caused by reusing the same storage location for two computations, by mapping the second computation into hidden locations.
A dataflow issue scheme sending instructions to reservation stations that hold operand values, or tags of the stations that will produce still-unavailable operands.
A centralised or distributed buffer that manages out-of-order execution by holding results until the sequential state order is restored.
The delay to read or write storage, largely a function of physical parameters such as processor–storage distance, bus delay, and chip delay.
The ability of the memory to respond to requests per unit time; with access time, one of the two basic parameters determining memory-system performance.
An array of floating-gate transistors whose trapped floating-gate charge provides non-volatile storage, with a limited number (usually below a million) of reliable rewrite cycles.
A small, fast (one-cycle access) memory holding frequently used or anticipated instructions and data, managed directly by the programmer.
A processor reference not found in the cache; the cache then fetches the missing data, as an associated region of memory called a line, from memory.
A cache mapping in which each main-memory block is mapped to exactly one cache location; easy to implement but not flexible.
A compromise mapping in which each block may reside in any of N locations of a set, easing direct-mapping contention while reducing the size of the associative search.
A cache write policy in which a replaced line is written back to memory only if it is dirty; used by most larger caches.
A cache line replacement policy that replaces the line least recently accessed by a read or write when the cache is full.
Separate instruction and data caches that double the access bandwidth of the cache ensemble, though a unified cache of the same total size has a lower miss rate.
Embedded DRAM, an on-die memory compromise integrating high-speed, high-leakage logic transistors with lower-speed, lower-leakage memory transistors on the same die.
A processor–memory interaction model where a processor issues a request only after the previous is served, requests are uniformly distributed, and unserviced requests are discarded each memory cycle.
Traditional on-chip communication in which a shared global bus connects the blocks of a chip, scaling poorly as core counts grow.
Royalty-free open on-chip interconnect specification from Arm, widely used as the standard bus for connecting functional blocks on a chip.
Bus protocol with 64 to 1024-bit data paths in which a multiplexer grants access to one master at a time.
Subset of a high-performance on-chip bus protocol for designs with a single master.
Low-complexity bus for low-bandwidth control accesses, such as peripheral register interfaces, with no bursts and 32-bit low-frequency operation.
Third-generation Arm bus interface for high-frequency designs, separating address and data phases, supporting bursts and out-of-order responses to multiple outstanding addresses.
Extension of the third-generation Arm interface adding signalling for system-wide cache coherency, so several processors can share memory.
Fifth-generation Arm interconnect protocol with a redesigned high-speed transport layer meant to reduce congestion in highly scalable chips.
Architecture combining some of the flexibility of software with the performance of hardware by using flexible platforms such as FPGAs.
Changing one part of reconfigurable hardware while the rest of the device keeps its existing configuration.
Form of partial reconfiguration in which the rest of the device keeps running while one region is reloaded.
Form of partial reconfiguration in which the device pauses while the changed region is reloaded.
Reconfigurable design using larger functional blocks such as word-wide ALUs, efficient for word-width algorithms but wasteful when operand sizes mismatch.
Frequency of reloading the hardware, which carries a configuration time and energy cost that is spread more thinly when changes are slower.
Replicating an algorithm across one or more FPGAs so several computing units process different data at the same time.
Processor core implemented wholly by logic synthesis on programmable logic such as FPGAs, with a count limited only by device size.
Custom chip built for a specific purpose that runs faster and uses less power than programmable logic but cannot be reprogrammed and is costly to make.
Symmetric-key encryption standard from NIST, published in 2001 as a restricted variant of Rijndael, processing 128-bit blocks with 128, 192 or 256-bit keys.
Non-linear cipher step replacing each state byte through a fixed 8-bit lookup table derived from a finite-field inverse and an affine transformation.
Cipher step rotating the bytes of each state row by a different offset, so columns are not encrypted independently.
Cipher step applying an invertible linear transformation to each state column using a fixed finite-field matrix, spreading changes across the block.
Cipher step that XORs each state byte with the corresponding byte of the current round key, the only step using the key directly.
Widely used lossy image compression method with adjustable quality-versus-size trade-off, typically reaching about 10:1 compression with acceptable loss.
Operation converting each 8×8 pixel block from spatial values into frequency components, on which lossy image compression is built.
Division of each frequency coefficient by a constant followed by rounding to an integer, the main lossy step in the pipeline.
Reducing the resolution of the colour-difference components, commonly 4:2:0, because the eye is less sensitive to fine colour detail.
Joint development of chip hardware and software, assembling pre-qualified IP blocks with EDA tools, then synthesis, place and route, and tape-out, with heavy verification.
